![Stage 2 — AI Refined Business Analyst Specification](https://www.appzar.com.ar/assets/molten-ai/step2-ai-refinement.webp)
---
## 4. Stages 3 & 4: Schema-Enforced Role Breakdown & Interactive Task Editor
Once the refined brief is approved, **Stage 3 (`Task Breakdown` — `/api/generate-tasks`)** uses the Vercel AI SDK (`generateObject`) with strict **Zod schemas** to synthesize cross-functional tasks across four specialized team roles (**`developer`**, **`designer`**, **`qa`**, and **`product-manager`**), complete with **Fibonacci effort estimates** (`1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21`), domain tags, and explicit inter-task dependencies (`Dependencies: developer-002`, etc.):
```typescript const taskSchema = z.object({ tasks: z.array( z.object({ id: z.string(), title: z.string(), summary: z.string(), effort: z.number(), // Fibonacci scale: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21 role: z.enum(["developer", "designer", "qa", "product-manager"]), tags: z.array(z.string()), dependencies: z.array(z.string()), status: z.enum(["todo", "in-progress", "review", "done"]).default("todo"), }), ), }) ```
![Stage 3 — Generated Role-Based Tasks with Fibonacci Effort & Dependencies](https://www.appzar.com.ar/assets/molten-ai/step3-task-breakdown.webp)
Directly addressing the market survey's top concern around **AI accuracy and human control**, **Stage 4 (`Edit Tasks`)** lets users review, customize, add, or prune any generated task before committing API credits to deep enrichment.
---
## 5. Stages 5 & 6: Credit-Gated Governance & Recursive Epic Decomposition
Because recursive LLM calls can multiply token costs, **Stage 5 (`Enrichment Configuration`)** introduces explicit **Credit & Complexity Governance**:
- **Enrichment Presets**: Choose between *Skip Enrichment* (`0 credits`), *Light Enrichment* (`~6 credits`, basic decomposition only), or *Full Enrichment* (`~18 credits`, complete decomposition + micro-todo generation). - **Fibonacci Complexity Threshold**: Tasks with effort $\ge$ the selected Fibonacci threshold (default: **8 points**) are flagged as too complex for a single sprint and automatically decomposed into an **Epic** with 3–5 smaller sub-tasks. - **Maximum Iterations Cap**: Bounds the recursion depth (e.g., `3 iterations`) to prevent infinite decomposition loops while displaying live estimated credits, cost, and processing time.
![Stage 5 — Enrichment Configuration, Complexity Threshold & Credit Budget](https://www.appzar.com.ar/assets/molten-ai/step5-enrichment-config.webp)
During **Stage 6 (`Task Enrichment`)**, `/api/decompose-to-epic` and `/api/enrich-task-advanced` iterate over the backlog: 1. Every task $\ge 8$ points is promoted to an **Epic** and split into 3–5 independently deliverable sub-tasks ($\le 8$ points). 2. Each atomic task is enriched with role-specific acceptance criteria, Definition of Done, and a prioritized **5–8 item todo checklist** where each action item is scoped to **15–60 minutes**.
---
## 6. Stage 7: Enhanced Kanban Board & Real-Time Project Analytics
Finally, the enriched backlog is rendered on the **Enhanced Project Kanban Board** (`To Do`, `In Progress`, `Review`, `Done`) with drag-and-drop status transitions, export/share actions, and a live **Project Statistics & Real-Time Analytics** dashboard tracking total tasks, story points, active epics, estimated working days, and role/priority distributions:
![Stage 7 — Enhanced Project Kanban Board](https://www.appzar.com.ar/assets/molten-ai/step6-kanban-board.webp)
![Real-Time Project Statistics, Role Distribution & Timeline Analytics](https://www.appzar.com.ar/assets/molten-ai/project-analytics.webp)
---
## Links & Resources
- **GitHub Repository**: [**github.com/daniazar/molten-ai-agent**](https://github.com/daniazar/molten-ai-agent) - **Consultancy**: [**MoltenMinds (moltenminds.com)**](https://moltenminds.com/)

item.title: Discord Schedule Bot: Coordinating Global UTC Community Events with Slash Commands & Supabase Realtime
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Building a dual-interface event scheduling system combining Discord.js v14 slash commands (/add) with a live Next.js + Supabase Realtime web dashboard for global gaming and engineering communities.
item.content:encoded:
Coordinating multiplayer matches or engineering syncs across four continents in Discord is notoriously chaotic: someone posts a time in EST, someone else replies in CET, messages scroll off-screen, and nobody knows which hour actually has a full lobby.
I built **[discord-schedule-bot](https://github.com/daniazar/discord-schedule-bot)** to give distributed Discord communities a deterministic, UTC-normalized scheduling engine that works simultaneously inside Discord via **Slash Commands** and on the web via a **live Supabase Realtime Dashboard**.
![Discord Schedule Bot Live Web Dashboard](https://www.appzar.com.ar/assets/discord-schedule-bot/dashboard.webp)
---
## 1. Dual-Interface Architecture: Discord Slash Commands + Web Matrix
The system shares a single PostgreSQL database (`titles` and `signups` tables in **Supabase**) across two synchronized interfaces:
1. **In-Channel Discord Bot (`bot.ts`)**: * Built with **`discord.js` v14**, registering guild/global slash commands via `scripts/register-commands.ts`. * Running `/add <hour>` (0–23 UTC) or `/title <event_name>` inside any Discord channel records the user's availability for that specific channel's event and posts an updated embed table grouped by UTC hour and day of the week. 2. **Interactive Next.js Web Dashboard (`pages/dashboard.tsx`)**: * Allows community members to view all active channel lobbies, filter by channel or participant, add or remove time slots directly from the browser, and export the full schedule to CSV.
---
## 2. Sub-Second Synchronization with Supabase Realtime
What makes the dashboard feel alive is its **Supabase Realtime (`postgres_changes`)** subscription pipeline:
```typescript const signupsSubscription = supabase .channel('signups_changes') .on('postgres_changes', { event: '*', schema: 'public', table: 'signups' }, () => { loadData(false); // Refresh lobby matrix without UI flicker }) .subscribe(); ```
When a player types `/add 20` inside a Discord text channel, the Next.js web dashboard updates the `20:00 UTC` participant badges in under 200ms over WebSockets—and when an organizer edits a slot on the web dashboard, the bot's state stays 100% consistent.

item.title: Property Manager: Engineering an Offline-First Rental Portfolio & Lease Suite with IndexedDB
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: How I built a local-first real estate portfolio manager in Next.js, TypeScript, Recharts, and IndexedDB to track rental properties, multi-step lease escalations, tenant payments, property taxes, and encrypted Google Drive backups.
item.content:encoded:
Managing a portfolio of rental properties involves surprisingly intricate financial state: leases have multi-tier step-up rent escalations (`rentSteps`), property taxes compound annually (`taxIncrementPercent`), some expenses are paid by the owner while others pass through to the tenant (`tenantPaysTaxes`), and payments settle across multiple bank accounts and currencies.
Most landlords end up maintaining fragile Excel spreadsheets because cloud SaaS property management platforms charge per-unit monthly fees and lock sensitive financial records inside proprietary databases.
To solve this, I built **[Property Manager](https://github.com/daniazar/property-manager)**—an **offline-first Single-Page Application** built with Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI, and **IndexedDB** (`propManagerDB`) that runs entirely in the browser with instant local persistence, full undo/redo state history, JSON snapshot portability, and optional Google Drive backup sync.
![Property Manager Financial Dashboard — Real-time portfolio KPIs, cashflow projections, and upcoming rent collections](https://www.appzar.com.ar/assets/property-manager/dashboard.webp)
---
## 1. Why IndexedDB (`propManagerDB` v4) Instead of a Cloud Database?
Financial and lease records are deeply personal. By designing a custom typed IndexedDB storage engine (`lib/storage-service.ts`) across ten relational object stores (`properties`, `accounts`, `transactions`, `payments`, `contracts`, `tenants`, `contacts`, `expenses`, `files`, and `history`), Property Manager achieves:
* **Zero Latency & 100% Offline Reliability**: Filtering transactions, projecting 12-month cashflows, and switching views execute in sub-millisecond memory/IndexedDB transactions. * **Complete Data Ownership (`/import-export`)**: The entire relational database can be exported as a single portable JSON snapshot or backed up to the user's personal Google Drive (`/api/google-drive`).
---
## 2. Portfolio Inventory & Automated Tax Projections
The **Properties** module (`app/properties/page.tsx`) tracks residential and commercial units alongside their purchase valuation, current market value, linked operating bank account, and recurring municipal taxes:
![Property Manager — Rental Property Portfolio View](https://www.appzar.com.ar/assets/property-manager/properties.webp)
Rather than requiring manual entry for recurring property tax bills, `generateTaxExpensesForProperty()` automatically synthesizes scheduled tax expense records and applies annual percentage escalations (`taxIncrementPercent`).
---
## 3. Multi-Step Lease Contracts (`rentSteps`)
In high-inflation or multi-year commercial/residential markets, rent is rarely flat for 36 months. The **Contracts** engine (`app/contracts/page.tsx`) models leases with an arbitrary array of time-bounded **`rentSteps`**:
![Property Manager — Active Lease Contracts with Multi-Step Rent Schedules](https://www.appzar.com.ar/assets/property-manager/contracts.webp)
Each contract links a property, one or more tenants (`tenantIds`), a realtor commission structure, security deposits, payment due days, and pass-through expense rules (`tenantPaysTaxes` / `tenantPaysOtherExpenses`).
---
## 4. Rent Collection Ledger & Cashflow Analytics
From active contracts, the **Payments** engine (`app/payments/page.tsx`) tracks monthly rent collection across `paid`, `pending`, and `overdue` states, automatically reconciling settled payments into the linked bank account's transaction ledger:
![Property Manager — Rent Payments & Collection Status](https://www.appzar.com.ar/assets/property-manager/payments.webp)
On the main dashboard (`app/page.tsx`), four interactive **Recharts** visualizations (`FutureCashflowChart`, `MonthlyIncomeExpenseBarChart`, `IncomeExpensesPieChart`, and `ExpenseBreakdownPieChart`) combine historical ledger transactions with future contract `rentSteps` to give an accurate 12-month forward cashflow projection.

item.title: Modding Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition for 4K UltraWide Displays
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Designing a custom 4K UltraWide HUD mod for Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition—clustering minimap, resources, and command panels into the bottom-left focal zone with transparent overlays and live JSON hot-reloading.
item.content:encoded:
Playing **Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition** on a large **4K or UltraWide monitor** is visually breathtaking—you can see massive swathes of your eco, woodlines, and incoming raids on a single screen. However, the default HUD layout was designed around standard 16:9 1080p viewing angles:
- **Resources and idle villager counters** sit far in the top-left corner. - **Unit command cards and production queues** sit in the bottom-left and top-left. - **The minimap and player scores** sit all the way in the bottom-right corner.
On a 4K display, checking your wood/food count, glanced against the minimap and unit queues, forces constant diagonal eye travel across the entire monitor. To solve this for my own competitive games, I built [**UI of Daniel Azar (`dani-ui-age2de`)**](https://github.com/daniazar/dani-ui-age2de) (published on the official Age of Empires Mod Workshop as [**Mod #16939**](https://www.ageofempires.com/mods/details/16939)).
![UI of Daniel Azar — 4K UltraWide HUD Layout](https://www.appzar.com.ar/assets/aoe2-ui-mod.webp)
---
## Design Goals: Zero-Eye-Travel Ergonomics
Inspired by competitive RTS layouts (such as Redi UI 3), I redesigned the widget coordinates around three principles:
1. **Bottom-Left & Center Focal Clustering**: Move the minimap (`mappanel.json`), resource bar (`resourcepanel.json`), command panel (`commandpanel.json`), and unit/technology production queues (`technologyprogresspanel.json`) into a tight, unified cluster along the bottom-left and lower-center of the screen. 2. **Transparent HUD Panels**: Replace opaque stone borders and heavy decorative frames with clean, semi-transparent overlays (`widgetui/textures/`) so terrain, units, and elevation remain visible underneath the UI. 3. **Unobstructed Center Viewport**: Keep the upper 80% of the 4K canvas completely clear of chrome so macro eco management and micro unit control have maximum screen real estate.
---
## Anatomy of Age of Empires II: DE's `widgetui` System
Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition drives its entire in-game HUD through declarative JSON layout files inside the `widgetui/` directory. Each panel is controlled by a dedicated JSON configuration:
| Widget File | In-Game HUD Responsibility | Key Customizations in `dani-ui-age2de` | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `commandpanel.json` | Main building/unit action grid & stances | Anchored bottom-left with stripped ornamental frames | | `mappanel.json` | Interactive minimap, flare & filter buttons | Relocated from bottom-right to bottom-left beside command panel | | `resourcepanel.json` | Wood, Food, Gold, Stone, Pop & Idle Villagers | Repositioned directly above the lower HUD cluster for instant glances | | `technologyprogresspanel.json` | Active unit & technology research queues | Stacked cleanly above the command card | | `scorepanel.json` | Diplomacy & live player score breakdown | Compacted with transparent backdrop | | `worldtimerpanel.json` | In-game clock, F11 FPS & game speed | Tucked cleanly next to the lower focal area | | `dialogquickchat.json` | Quick-chat & taunt overlay | Adjusted coordinates to avoid overlapping relocated panels |
```mermaid flowchart LR A["Top-Left Legacy Bar\nResources + Tech Queue"] -->|Relocate Down| D["Unified Bottom-Left / Center Cluster\nCommand Panel + Resource Bar + Tech Queue + Minimap"] B["Bottom-Right Legacy Corner\nMinimap + Score Panel"] -->|Relocate Left| D C["Opaque Stone Textures"] -->|Replace in widgetui/textures| E["Transparent HUD Overlays\nMax 4K Battlefield Visibility"] ```
---
## The Live Hot-Reload Trick for UI Modders
One of the most frustrating parts of modding `widgetui` coordinates on 4K resolutions is the edit-launch-test loop: normally, if you bundle both textures and `.json` files inside a single local mod folder, you have to restart a skirmish match every time you tweak an `x` or `y` pixel offset.
While building this mod, I used a two-tier workflow that gives **instant live hot-reloading** inside a running match:
1. **Isolate Custom Textures in the Local Mod Folder**: Place everything *except* the `.json` layout files (such as transparent `.dds` / `.png` panel backgrounds inside `widgetui/textures/`) into your local subscribed/local mod directory. 2. **Edit `.json` Layout Files Directly in the Base Game Folder**: While the game is running in a skirmish match, edit the corresponding `commandpanel.json`, `mappanel.json`, or `resourcepanel.json` directly inside the game's installation `widgetui/` directory. 3. **Instant In-Game Refresh**: The engine watches the base `widgetui/*.json` files and applies coordinate/size changes live without reloading the game—turning hours of blind pixel guessing into a fast, interactive layout session.
---
## Try It Out or Customize Your Own
- **In-Game Mod Workshop**: Search for **Daniel Azar** in the Age of Empires II: DE Mod Manager or view [**Mod #16939 on ageofempires.com**](https://www.ageofempires.com/mods/details/16939). - **Source & JSON Layouts**: Clone or fork [**github.com/daniazar/dani-ui-age2de**](https://github.com/daniazar/dani-ui-age2de) to tweak the panel coordinates for your own monitor resolution.

item.title: LSystemTS: Rendering Recursive Lindenmayer Fractals & Space-Filling Curves in TypeScript
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Following up on publishing turtle-ts to npm by building lsystemts—a recursive Lindenmayer System grammar interpreter that renders Sierpinski Triangles, Koch Snowflakes, and Hilbert Space-Filling Curves on HTML5 Canvas.

item.title: Deploying my first typescript library
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Writing modular code is a good idea. And nothing is more modular than writing a library. How can you write a TypeScript library? Well, that's exactly what this tutorial is about! This tutorial works with TypeScript 3.x
item.content:encoded:
Writing modular code is a good idea. And nothing is more modular than writing a library. How can you write a TypeScript library? Well, that's exactly what this tutorial is about! This tutorial works with TypeScript 3.x
In my case I wanted to play a little with L-System and fractals. To achieve this first we need a Turtle Graphics engine. I didnt found one for typescript so i made one and published it to NPM registry. I will assume you already know how to create a typescript project.
## Create an index.ts file Add an index.ts file to your src folder. Its purpose is to export all the parts of the library you want to make available for consumers. In my case it would simply be:
``` export { Color } from "./Color"; export { Figure } from "./Figure"; export { Point } from "./Point"; export { Turtle } from "./Turtle"; ```
## Configure the package.json The package name is what the consumer is going to use to import functionality from your library later on. The whole package.json would look like so:
typescript-library/package.json ``` { "name": "turtle-ts", "version": "2.0.0", "description": "Turtle graphics engine in typescript", "main": "dist/index.js", "types": "dist/index.d.ts", "scripts": { "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1" }, "repository": { "type": "git", "url": "git+https://github.com/daniazar/turtlets.git" }, "keywords": [ "turtle", "engine", "typescript" ], "author": "Daniel Azar", "license": "MIT", "bugs": { "url": "https://github.com/daniazar/turtlets/issues" }, "homepage": "https://github.com/daniazar/turtlets#readme", "dependencies": { "eslint": "^7.2.0" } } ```
The package name you choose will be used by people for their imports, so choose wisely!
There's also one all-important flag in this package.json: You have to declare where to find the type declarations! This is done using "types": "dist/index.d.ts" Otherwise the consumer won't find your module!
## Configure .npmignore If you would compile your code now with tsc and run npm publish, you'd publish the dist folder along with all the other files. However, you don't really need the source folder. To avoid publishing unnecessary files to npm, you can create an .npmignore file. In our case it's simple:
``` tsconfig.json src ``` As your project grows, you will need to ignore more files, for example test files.
Step 6: Publish to npm To publish your first version to npm run:
``` tsc npm init npm publish ```
Now you're all set to go! Consume the library anywhere you want. in this case by running:
``` npm install --save turtle-ts ```
For subsequent releases, use the semvar principle. When you make a patch / bugfix to your library, you can run npm version patch, for new features run npm version minor and on breaking changes of your api run npm version major.

item.title: Lessons Learnt with TV Master
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Problems and solutions found while making a tv streaming site.
item.content:encoded:
> CORS and security measures cause a lot of trouble in not common scenarios.
Hi, this is a continuation of the last TV Master post. To explain most of the issues and solutions I encountered upon making the TV Master site.
The first issue i had was a security issue with the **iframe**. The problem appears when adding an HTTPS iframe to an HTTP website or vice versa. In one case the browser refuse to load it, while in the other it prompts the user to allow it. The prompt is not easily visible so its easy to miss. Also on mobile browsers there is no prompt.
![example unsafe iframe](https://www.appzar.com.ar/images/unsafe.jpg)
The solution is to use HTTPS on your site with the appropriate certificate. if you need help making a certificate read the post title **title: Easily create a SSL certificate**. The other way around is blocked automatically by most browsers.
Then we go into iframes permissions. you could enable or block popups, javascript, redirects, etc. The implementation of this appears to differ for each major browser. I would like to block redirects popups to block Ads but need to leave javascript as most videos streams don't use the HTML5 video tag. The best browser handling this issues appear to be **Opera**.
We begin with CORS. ![example unsafe iframe](https://www.appzar.com.ar/images/cors2.png) With CORS on the server side you can enable or block other sites from using your resources. this could be done by IP, Origins Domain, etc. As times go by more providers block their signals so they cant be played on other websites. This is really cumbersome as we don't have control over the browser origin url arguments on requests. if we had we could do easily Cross Site Scripting hacks. There are two ways to bypass this, having a backend server acting as proxy or not using a browser as the frontend. But the app was already started and the architecture and languages chosen.
Then we used electron. An Electron app is a web engine encapsulated website with access to the relaying OS. Electron by default doesn't help us violating web security. but with some tinkering lets us bypass CORS by setting origin URL per request as whatever we want. In Electron we need to change the iFrame tags to WebViews tags for security to prevent the iframe from accessing the relaying OS features. So the web and Desktop implementation needs to differ with the App having better functionality.
I think that covers the big issues presented while developing this App.

item.title: Automating Enterprise Firewall Migrations in Go: Cisco ASA to Check Point VSX
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: How we built open-source Go CLI parsers at MoltenMinds to convert thousands of Cisco ASA sub-interfaces, static routes, and outbound ACL rules into Check Point VSX & SmartMove policy packages without manual rule breakage.
item.content:encoded:
During enterprise security migrations at [**MoltenMinds**](https://moltenminds.com/), one of the most error-prone operational tasks we encountered was migrating legacy **Cisco ASA** perimeter and data-center firewalls over to **Check Point VSX (Virtual System Extension)** appliances.
When a data center firewall has accumulated years of VLAN sub-interfaces (`Port-channel1.340`), hundreds of static routes, and thousands of Access Control Lists (ACLs), migrating those policies by hand is a recipe for midnight outages. Even worse, vendor migration tools like **Check Point SmartMove** choke or drop policies when encountering **Cisco ASA outbound ACL rules (`access-list ... out`)**, because Check Point's policy model evaluates interface directionality differently during import.
To eliminate manual translation errors and turn multi-day migration windows into repeatable 5-second builds, we engineered two open-source CLI tools in **Go**: 1. [**`ASAtoVSXParser`**](https://github.com/MoltenMinds/ASAtoVSXParser) — Parses raw Cisco ASA configuration dumps into structured JSON interface and routing tables ready for Check Point VSX provisioning. 2. [**`FW-ASA-ACL-Out-Rule-Converter`**](https://github.com/MoltenMinds/FW-ASA-ACL-Out-Rule-Converter) — Rewrites SmartMove-exported ASA Outbound ACL rules into equivalent Inbound route-aware policy scripts so Check Point management servers import 100% of the rulebase cleanly.
---
## Problem 1: Extracting Virtual Interfaces & Routes (`ASAtoVSXParser`)
A typical Cisco ASA configuration interleaves physical port channels, VLAN sub-interfaces, security levels, `nameif` aliases, and static routes across thousands of lines:
```text interface Port-channel1.340 description INSIDE_93_DCINT_MAN_RFG_MINTRANS_EXCH vlan 340 nameif INSIDE_93_DCINT_MAN_RFG_MINTRANS_EXCH security-level 30 ip address 10.240.115.98 255.255.255.248
route OUTSIDE 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 181.209.69.246 1 ```
In [**`ASAtoVSXParser`**](https://github.com/MoltenMinds/ASAtoVSXParser), we built a single-pass line scanner in Go (`runner.go`) that tokenizes interface stanzas and `route` declarations into strongly typed `models.Port` and `models.Route` structs, correlating each `nameif` alias with its CIDR netmask and VLAN tag, and emitting clean `-interfaces.json` and `-routes.json` artifacts for automated VSX provisioning.
---
## Problem 2: The Outbound ACL Trap in Check Point SmartMove
When you run **Check Point SmartMove (`v5.1+`)** against a Cisco ASA configuration that relies heavily on **Outbound ACLs** (rules attached to an egress interface via `access-group ... out interface ...`), SmartMove flags or fails to import those rules cleanly because standard gateway rulebases expect ingress-normalized topology mappings.
```mermaid flowchart LR A["Cisco ASA Config\nSub-Interfaces + Outbound ACLs"] --> B["Check Point SmartMove\nRaw Policy Script Export"] B --> C["FW-ASA-ACL-Out-Rule-Converter\nGo Stream Transformer"] C --> D["Normalized Inbound ACL Script\n100% Clean Management Import"] ```
To solve this without manually rewriting hundreds of firewall rules: - [**`FW-ASA-ACL-Out-Rule-Converter`**](https://github.com/MoltenMinds/FW-ASA-ACL-Out-Rule-Converter) ingests the script generated by Check Point SmartMove. - It scans the header, rulebase, and footer boundaries, automatically transforming **ASA Outbound ACL rules** into normalized **Inbound route rules** while preserving source/destination networks, service ports, logging flags, and rule ordering. - The resulting `-output.txt` script can be executed directly on the **Check Point Management Server** to create the complete policy package with zero import errors.
---
## Why Go for SecDevOps Tooling?
For network security engineers working inside locked-down jump hosts and air-gapped management networks, Python or Node.js scripts that require installing external runtime dependencies (`pip` / `npm`) are a non-starter. Compiling our parsers in **Go** using only the standard library (`bufio`, `os`, `strings`, `encoding/json`) meant we could cross-compile a single zero-dependency static binary (`GOOS=windows` or `GOOS=linux`), drop it onto any migration workstation, and process tens of thousands of firewall lines in milliseconds.
Both tools are available on the MoltenMinds GitHub organization: - [**github.com/MoltenMinds/ASAtoVSXParser**](https://github.com/MoltenMinds/ASAtoVSXParser) - [**github.com/MoltenMinds/FW-ASA-ACL-Out-Rule-Converter**](https://github.com/MoltenMinds/FW-ASA-ACL-Out-Rule-Converter)

item.title: Fixing old images
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: During the COVID-19 pandemic we all have a lot more time at home that what we used to. How i applied some of that time on postponed tasks.
item.content:encoded:
During the COVID-19 pandemic we all have a lot more time at home that what we used to. This is due to most countries implementing a quarantine. To better use this time I decided to finish some family projects that were always postponed by other things. This time we are talking about digitalizing all the old photos inside our home.
For this project we used a Fujitsu ScanSnap iX500. once all the photo albums were scanned we found to big issues.
1. Decoloration of old pictures. usually a red tint. 2. if merged with google photos or other system all the pictures metadata is wrong.
## Decoloration This will be the subject of a following post that includes an IA Neural Network to fix them.
## Metadata
An image file can contain several information regarding the time and mechanism when it was taken. We don't think about this data as most smartphones manage this information correctly now a days. But for old photos its a different paradigm.
Most photos software wont let you edit this metadata or just edit it once at a time. That can be an issue if you have as many photos as I do.
![Amount of pictures](https://www.appzar.com.ar/images/scanned-folder.png)
To fix this i searched for programs or ways to do it but all had complex interfaces or didn't work as expected on every file. So I decided to make my own application to fix them. The app ended being a Windows 10 application using WinUI 3.0 Alpha. because of the alpha status some of the common components like a map was not working.
The metadata that I wanted to fix the most was the date taken tag and the location of the picture. As I already have them separated by albums we could assume in most cases that all the pictures in an album were taken on the same period / location. So the app lets you choose one picture or a folder and process one at a time or all together.
You input the location, that gets converted using Bing Maps API for windows to coordinates. The location can be a full address or just a city or country.
![application running](https://www.appzar.com.ar/images/image-metadata.png)
If you want to check the application code it is located at my GitHub account.

item.title: Issues when using configuration files in Scaling environments
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Dealing with issues on Azure Blob Storage throttling, Redis cache failover, and exponential retry policies in multi-region scaled environments.
item.content:encoded:
Hello,
We will continue our last post on problems that appear when scaling. This time we want to talk about what happens when you need to use configuration parameters in an environment. These values can be stored in many different places. In the case of the project we had, they were stored in [**Azure Blob Storage**](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/services/storage/blobs/). The problem in this case appeared when enabling auto scaling.
## About the project
First we need to explain the project. It was a complex backend application in **C#**. The architecture of the project was designed with scaling in mind. It consisted of Frontend and Backend App Service Servers. Each server contained many WebJobs. The different WebJobs needed several parameters to run correctly. When they were launched each one needed to read a configuration file containing these parameters.
We decided to use configuration files instead of saving the values directly to the database, first because of a performance issue, but also to be able to have different sets of parameters for each region and environment. These values could be changed from the frontend so each job had to refresh them after some time so the changes propagate across the app in a similar way that DNS changes propagate.
To read the files we had three checks: first we search in local memory cache for the file. Then we search in [**Redis**](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/services/cache/) — if not present we look for the file in [**Azure Blob Storage**](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/services/storage/blobs/).
With this architecture the program was already running in multiple regions with multiple servers. And in each region it was configured with App Service using a considerable number of instances.
## The Problem
The Application was working as expected. And a new objective was defined to reduce the costs. After solving the scaling problems we started to find a couple times during two-week periods where the program was logging errors when accessing the configuration files.
At first we thought there was a problem with Azure Redis and Blob Storage both at the same time, but the issue happened again after some time and that couldn't be a coincidence. Then we started to investigate the possible cause of the issue.
## The solution
After days of reading what could cause these reading errors when accessing the configuration files, the first thing we could correlate was our errors with the downtimes of the Redis cache service. So we now knew that each server could have at most 20 instances, and these instances had more than 30 jobs, so we had at most 600 processes running a request asking for the file. That is if every instance was started at the same time. So why would the Blob Storage fail for 600 file requests?
We found the [**documentation**](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/scalability-targets) on scalability and performance for Blob storage. There we can see that there is a throttle limit independent of the Storage tier you have. This limit is 500 requests per second, which we were hitting sometimes; even with our retry policy we were having errors.
The retry policy was waiting for a constant time; upon changing it to an exponential backoff policy, most of the issues were resolved.
Then we read about the [**naming convention**](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/blobs/storage-performance-checklist#partitioning) to improve Storage Service load balancing. We were saving in the same Storage account all the queue messages and leasing files without appropriate naming. Upon changing that we resolved all the issues with the blob services.
Hope you learnt something about managing Blob files in a scaling application.
Regards.

item.title: The Hurdles of auto scaling an Application to reduce costs
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Lessons learnt on scaling a cloud designed application.
item.content:encoded: Hello everyone, We are going to share our experience when enabling auto scale in a cloud designed application. In this case a series a problems surged while enabling auto scale. We find this happen on several projects from different clients. So we hope you can learn from common mistakes and save time when deploying your next application. I'm also looking to see what is your approach in this matter. Important: This post is mainly focused on a case using **Azure App Service** but it has a correlation to any environment where you can Scale automatically or manual a cloud application or service. ## About the project First we need to explain the project. It was a complex backend application in **C#**. The architecture of the project was design with scaling in mind. It consisted of Frontend and Backend App Service Servers. Each server contained many Webjobs. A series of Queues with different messages were used to communicate between the Webjobs and frontend with backend. There was a number of retry attempts in case of errors processing the messages and poison queues. With this architecture the program already was running in multiple regions with multiple servers. And in each region it was configured with App Service using a considerable number of instances. ## The Proposal The Application was working as expected. And a new objective was defined to reduce the costs. To achieve this we needed to make each region capable to adapt the number of instances based on demand. App Service provides two modes to scale: * Automatic * Manual Automatic mode scales instances based on the load of CPU. This could be useful for a frontend or CPU intensive tasks but not for our case. In our case our load was based on the amount of messages in queues. We decided to use the manual option. Using the API to manage the number of instances we implemented a custom logic to scale the number of instances. The algorithm scaled up if queue depth increased beyond custom limits for the number of instances. | Queue Depth | Number of instances | | ----------- | ------------------- | | 10 | 2 | | 40 | 4 | | 80 | 8 | | 200 | 12 | | 500 | 16 | | 1000 | 20 | To decrease the number of instances it waits a few minutes in case the surge goes back up. This is because the time to spin a new server usually goes over 90 seconds. We don't want to decrease just to increase it again in the next minute. ## The Problem After these changes were deployed to production for a few days we started to notice a couple of strange errors. At first when debugging some errors in the logs there were cases when we followed the flow of the logging messages for a request message chains it wab broken. It suddenly stops in a random place. We knew this was an issue but couldn't find the reason. Then after a few weeks we found a couple of requests whose messages status were inconsistent. It appeared like it was added to a following step queue but retained the status as not processed. Upon further inspection the same random stop of logging messages were found. This was a severe issue now cause we had to guarantee that the 100% of queue messages were processed correctly or at least send an error notification to the client. ## The solution After a couple of days of reading and learning what could cause this sudden interrupts. We found that the App Service hold logs that were not present in Application Insights Logs. We started correlating the logs event dates to the auto scaling and found that they occurred after the down scale of a server. Once we could identify the root cause of the problem. We could start attacking the issue. We found that we couldn't decide which server instance was going to be shutdown when down scaling. But we could implement a graceful shutdown. A graceful shutdown means that App Service send a signal to the process running on the server thats going to be shutdown. We added a custom logic with semaphores to prevent the WebJobs from starting to process new messages from queues once shutdown signal was sent. As the operations of enqueueing a message and changing its status in the database were not atomic we had to prevent any WebJob after the graceful shutdown signal from doing this operations. This way we ensure no data remained inconsistent. This way we resolved the main issues generated by the journey of auto scale. There were others problems that surged but we will cover them in another post. Hope you learnt something from one of the most common mistakes during scale of an application. Regards.

item.title: Launching MoltenMinds: Building a Cloud, SecDevOps & Engineering Consultancy
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: How we teamed up to launch MoltenMinds—an engineering consultancy focused on tackling hard IT problems across Cloud Architecture (Azure, AWS, GCP), SecDevOps, Infrastructure Automation, and Distributed Systems.
item.content:encoded:
Over the last couple of years, working across large-scale backend architectures, distributed cloud deployments, and enterprise security infrastructure, a recurring pattern kept surfacing: companies rarely struggle with writing standard CRUD logic—they struggle where **software architecture meets cloud infrastructure, security, and scale**.
When a multi-region system starts dropping messages silently during scale-in events, or when TLS inspection appliances bottleneck throughput across hybrid cloud networks, having separate "developers", "cloud ops", and "security auditors" working in silos slows root-cause analysis to a crawl.
That is why we decided to join forces and launch [**MoltenMinds**](https://moltenminds.com/)—a dedicated engineering consultancy built around a simple premise: **We are IT Problem Solvers.**
---
## Who We Are
We built [**MoltenMinds**](https://moltenminds.com/) by combining three complementary engineering backgrounds into a single tight-knit team:
- **Daniel Azar** — *Software Design Engineer*: Focused on distributed backend architectures (C# / .NET, Java, Node.js, Python), cloud auto-scaling, high-throughput messaging queues, and full-stack application engineering. - **Federico Meiners** — *CyberSecurity Architect*: Focused on enterprise network security, SecDevOps pipelines, HTTPS/SSL inspection, and cloud security posture across hybrid environments. - **Santiago Arroyo** — *Software Engineer*: Focused on systems integration, cloud-native deployments, automation tooling, and resilient backend services.
Whether a client needs help untangling a legacy deployment, designing a multi-region cloud architecture from scratch, or hardening their infrastructure with real **SecDevOps** practices, our goal is to jump into the hardest part of the stack and engineer a clean, measurable fix.
---
## Our Three Core Pillars
At [**MoltenMinds**](https://moltenminds.com/), our work centers on three intersecting pillars:
### 1. Cloud Architecture & Cost-Aware Scaling (Azure, AWS & Google Cloud) Moving to the cloud is easy; running a multi-region cloud deployment without burning unnecessary budget or losing data under burst load is the real challenge. We design and audit workloads across **Microsoft Azure**, **AWS**, and **Google Cloud**—ranging from custom queue-depth auto-scaling engines on Azure App Service and WebJobs to multi-tier caching strategies with Redis and Blob Storage.
### 2. Cybersecurity & Real SecDevOps Security shouldn't be a checklist bolted on at the end of a release cycle. We focus on pragmatic **SecDevOps**: embedding security controls, automated certificate lifecycle management, deep HTTPS/SSL inspection (such as Check Point gateway inspection pipelines), and least-privilege cloud IAM directly into CI/CD and infrastructure code.
### 3. Deep Systems Integration & Automation Modern architectures rarely live in a single vendor's ecosystem. We build the glue and automation layers that let disparate services, identity providers, message brokers, and monitoring stacks operate as one cohesive platform.
---
## How We Work: Iterative Engineering
Every tough infrastructure or architecture problem looks murky at first—whether it is intermittent storage throttling or broken trace logs across 20 cloud instances. Instead of guessing or throwing larger VM SKUs at a bottleneck, we follow a strict iterative engineering loop:
```mermaid flowchart LR A["1. Analyze Issues\nTelemetry, Logs & Root Cause"] --> B["2. Design Solution\nCloud & SecDevOps Architecture"] B --> C["3. Automate & Integrate\nIaC, Graceful Lifecycle & CI/CD"] C --> D["4. Test & Validate\nLoad Testing & Cost Verification"] D -->|Iterate until goals are met| A ```
1. **Analyze the Issues**: We correlate telemetry across application logs, cloud platform diagnostics, cache downtime windows, and network boundaries to isolate the exact root cause rather than treating symptoms. 2. **Design a Solution**: We architect a targeted fix—such as semaphore-driven graceful shutdown hooks for scale-in events, or partition-aware naming conventions and exponential backoff policies for cloud storage. 3. **Automate & Integrate**: We codify the solution into repeatable deployments so manual operational toil disappears. 4. **Test & Repeat**: We verify the fix under real production load and iterate until both reliability and cost-efficiency targets are reached.
---
## Sharing Our Field Notes
As part of launching [**MoltenMinds**](https://moltenminds.com/), we also want to document and share real-world post-mortems and architectural lessons from our client engagements (anonymized, of course) so other engineering teams can avoid the same pitfalls:
- [**The Hurdles of Auto Scaling an Application to Reduce Costs**](https://www.appzar.com.ar/posts/auto-scale-problems/) — How we designed a custom queue-depth auto-scaler in C# on Azure App Service and solved silent data corruption during instance scale-in using semaphore-based graceful shutdowns. - [**Issues When Using Configuration Files in Scaling Environments**](https://www.appzar.com.ar/posts/auto-scale-blob-storage/) — Tracking down a 600-process stampede during Redis failovers that hit Azure Blob Storage's 500 RPS throttle limit, and fixing it with exponential backoff and storage partition naming conventions.
If you are facing a complex cloud scaling bottleneck, a tricky SecDevOps integration, or a distributed systems mystery, check out [**moltenminds.com**](https://moltenminds.com/) or reach out to us on [**GitHub**](https://github.com/MoltenMinds).

item.title: WebScreen: Declarative Headless Chrome Screenshot & DOM Capture Automation
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Building a JSON-driven visual capture tool in TypeScript and Puppeteer to batch-render full webpages, responsive viewports, and isolated CSS selector crops.
item.content:encoded:
Whether you are generating visual regression snapshots across environments, archiving marketing pages, or extracting specific UI widgets for documentation, manually taking and cropping browser screenshots quickly becomes tedious.
To automate this workflow, I built [**WebScreen (`daniazar/webscreen`)**](https://github.com/daniazar/webscreen)—a declarative, JSON-driven screenshot engine written in **TypeScript** on top of **Headless Chrome and the Puppeteer API**.
---
## Declarative Capture via `url.json`
Instead of writing custom imperative Puppeteer scripts every time you need to capture a new site or component, **WebScreen** reads a declarative `url.json` manifest where each entry specifies: - **Full-Page or Viewport Capture** (`fullPage`, `capturePage`, custom `viewport.width` $\times$ `viewport.height`). - **Targeted DOM Element Crops (`elements`)**: An array of CSS selectors (`.class` or `#id`) that WebScreen locates in the live DOM, computes bounding boxes for, and exports as isolated image files. - **Output Format (`extension`)**: Supports lossless `png` or compressed `jpeg` output.
```json [ { "url": "https://github.com/", "name": "github", "fullPage": true, "capturePage": true, "elements": [ ".home-hero-signup" ], "extension": "jpeg" }, { "url": "https://google.com/", "viewport": { "width": 300, "height": 400 }, "capturePage": true, "elements": [ ".content", "#hplogo" ] } ] ```
---
## How the Capture Pipeline Works
```mermaid flowchart LR A["url.json Manifest\nURLs + Viewports + CSS Selectors"] --> B["Headless Chromium\nPuppeteer Page Instance"] B --> C["Viewport & Network Idle\nApply Width/Height & Wait for Render"] C --> D["Full-Page Snapshot\npage.screenshot({ fullPage })"] C --> E["DOM Selector Cropping\npage.$(selector) → element.screenshot()"] ```
For each target in `url.json`: 1. **Viewport Configuration**: If a custom `viewport` is defined (e.g., `300x400` to simulate a mobile device), WebScreen resizes the headless browser tab before navigation so responsive media queries trigger accurately. 2. **Page-Level Capture**: When `capturePage: true` is enabled, it captures either the visible viewport or the stitched `fullPage` scroll height. 3. **Sub-Element Isolation**: It iterates through the `elements` array, queries each CSS selector via `page.$(selector)`, and renders an exact bounding-box screenshot of that DOM node (`github_0.jpeg`, `google_1.png`, etc.).
The repository and documentation are available on GitHub at [**github.com/daniazar/webscreen**](https://github.com/daniazar/webscreen).

item.title: Easily create a SSL certificate
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: When developing an app you will need to use HTTPS more frequently as browser are blocking simple http requests and some tools stop working without a correct certificate. Generate your certificate easy with this guide.
item.content:encoded:
> Success is no accident. It is hard work, perseverance, learning, studying, sacrifice and most of all, love of what you are doing or learning to do. - Pele
# Generate a Trusted SSL Certificate
When developing an app you will need to use HTTPS more frequently as browser are blocking simple http requests and some tools stop working without a correct certificate. Also it is important when using Docker and micro services with your own registry.
Because of this you need to learn how to generate a certificate. The easiest option is to use OpenSSL to generate your own certificate, but its interface can be cumbersome. To streamline the use of it and not having to read documentation each time you can clone the following repository and invoke the script. It will generate a Certificate based on a configuration file with easy to understand values.
``` git clone https://github.com/daniazar/generate-trusted-ssl-certificate.git cd <PATH_TO_REPO_FOLDER>/generate-trusted-ssl-certificate bash generate.sh ```
## Requirements Install OpenSsl on your OS
# OS X You should be all set. OS X has by default openssl installed.
# Windows 10 Install openssl. I recommend using the Git bash. It has openssl preinstalled. Git Bash is bundled with the Git installer.
https://git-scm.com/
## Configuration
You can adjust the `[dn]` part of the `openssl-custom.cnf` file to whatever you prefer.
``` [dn] C = <COUNTRY> ST = <STATE> L = <LOCALITY / CITY> O = <ORGANIZATION> OU = <ORGANIZATION_UNIT> emailAddress = <EMAIL_ADDRESS> CN = <HOSTNAME / IP_ADDRESS> ```
## Angular In case of angular if you need to run ng serve with a secure port on development. This is the case for example if your application contains an iframe of a website with https.
To run angular cli with https use
``` ng serve --ssl true --ssl-cert server.crt --ssl-key server.key ```

item.title: Making an App to watch TV Channels
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Why I decided to make my own tv streaming site, and how i achieve it.
item.content:encoded:
> I grow tired of small rectangular streaming on sites and ads.
Hello guys, first a little about me. I don't like to hear music while working but i like having news, a movie or a tv show in the background. But with some channels I used in the past starting to add annoying Ads or timed refresh of the website, I needed a change. After looking around and not finding what i was looking. I decided it was time to make my own website to stream content. Just look at the following example:
![example of little video in news site](https://www.appzar.com.ar/images/america-tv.png)
> **Use Opera Web Browser** for TV Master to work best.
I decided to make the App. It started as a Web Application, using typescript and angular. The idea was to make it easy to watch and change channels. Make the video size nearly full site with the option to go Fullscreen. For the backend it uses firebase, for the database and the login. Admin users can change and add new channels, while the rest can report non working channels. As i don't host the streams they change frequently and it makes some channels to stop working. Added tabs to enable multiple sources per channel and a Guide button for each channel. Then added a calendar feature for events like sports and which channel it was available. Some of the sources could be easily added like Youtube live streams but others where a bit shady origin with some complex iframe programming to be added. Also each had to be easily edited on real time.
Example of the video adjusting its size to the windows width. With a limit on height. ![video in small window](https://www.appzar.com.ar/images/tvmaster-small.png)
Example of the video on max height. ![video in big window](https://www.appzar.com.ar/images/tvmaster-full.png)
Example of changing the channel without interrupting the video in the main view. ![video in big window](https://www.appzar.com.ar/images/tvmaster-channelpopup.png)
I will make another post explaining the problems faced and the learnt things.

item.title: CloudCam: Building a Smart Security Camera with Raspberry Pi & Real-Time Face Recognition
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Engineering an end-to-end IoT surveillance and biometric recognition platform combining a custom Raspberry Pi camera node, IP camera streams, AngularJS, PostgreSQL, and Kairos Face Recognition.
item.content:encoded:
Back in 2015, consumer security cameras were mostly passive DVR boxes—they could record hours of motion-triggered footage to an SD card or FTP server, but they couldn't tell the difference between a family member arriving home, a stray cat, or an unknown intruder.
To explore smart home automation and cloud biometrics, I built **CloudCam**—a unified smart security camera platform with **real-time face recognition**, supporting standard USB webcams, RTSP/HTTP IP cameras, and a custom **Raspberry Pi hardware camera prototype**.
---
## System Architecture: Edge Capture + Cloud Biometrics
CloudCam was designed around a three-tier architecture so inexpensive edge cameras could offload heavy biometric matching to a central backend:
```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Edge ["1. Camera Ingestion Layer"] A1["Custom Raspberry Pi Camera Node"] A2["Standard RTSP / HTTP IP Cameras"] A3["Local Webcams (WebRTC / Canvas)"] end subgraph Core ["2. CloudCam Backend & Storage"] B1["Motion & Frame Extraction Service"] B2["Kairos Face Recognition API\nEnrollment & Verification"] B3["PostgreSQL Database\nCamera Registry & Event Timeline"] end subgraph UI ["3. Real-Time Monitoring UI"] C1["AngularJS Web Dashboard\nLive Feeds, Known Faces & Alerts"] end Edge --> B1 B1 --> B2 B2 --> B3 B3 --> C1 ```
### 1. Universal Camera Ingestion & Raspberry Pi Node Instead of locking users into proprietary camera hardware, CloudCam allowed registering three types of video sources in a single dashboard: - **Custom Raspberry Pi Prototype**: A standalone Linux edge node equipped with the Raspberry Pi Camera Module that captured frames on motion events and streamed snapshots to the CloudCam server. - **IP Cameras**: Any standard network camera exposing an MJPEG or snapshot stream. - **Browser Webcams**: Instant zero-hardware testing directly from a laptop or spare phone camera.
### 2. Biometric Enrollment & Recognition via Kairos When CloudCam detected a person in frame, it extracted the image and dispatched it to the **Kairos Face Recognition** pipeline: - **Subject Enrollment**: Users could upload or tag reference photos of trusted family members or employees from the AngularJS dashboard to build a private gallery. - **Real-Time Identification**: Incoming camera frames were matched against the enrolled gallery, logging confidence scores, timestamps, and bounding-box snapshots in **PostgreSQL** and triggering instant alerts when an unrecognized face was detected.
---
## Video Walkthrough
You can watch the full live demonstration of the CloudCam web dashboard, face enrollment workflow, and Raspberry Pi camera prototype on YouTube: - [**Watch the CloudCam Demo on YouTube**](https://youtu.be/tSpp2GaxFvQ)

item.title: iSurfer Part 3: Inside the OpenGL ES 2.0 Fragment Shader Ray Tracer — Root Isolation, Safeguarded Newton-Bisection & Two-Sided Shading
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Part 3 of the iSurfer engineering deep-dive: how the GPU fragment shader clips viewing rays against a bounding sphere, isolates the first root along the ray, refines intersections with safeguarded Newton-Bisection, and shades two-sided algebraic manifolds in real time.

item.title: iSurfer Part 2: From Touch Input to GPU Silicon — The Equation Parser & On-the-Fly GLSL Shader Compiler
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Part 2 of the iSurfer engineering deep-dive: how our recursive-descent equation parser normalizes human algebraic notation into an Abstract Syntax Tree, expands integer powers to avoid IEEE pow() NaNs, computes symbolic partial derivatives, and JIT-compiles custom OpenGL ES 2.0 fragment shaders on the fly.

item.title: iSurfer Part 1: Why Implicit Algebraic Surfaces Demand Per-Pixel GPU Ray Tracing Over Polygon Meshes
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Part 1 of the iSurfer engineering deep-dive: why triangle polygonization algorithms like Marching Cubes fail at algebraic singularities, cusps, and self-intersections—and why casting continuous analytical rays per pixel on the GPU is the only way to achieve mathematical precision.
item.content:encoded:
When we began designing **iSurfer**—our undergraduate Computer Engineering thesis at **ITBA** (*Instituto Tecnológico de Buenos Aires*), inspired by the [**IMAGINARY**](https://www.imaginary.org/) open-mathematics platform and the Oberwolfach Research Institute's [**SURFER**](https://www.imaginary.org/program/surfer)—our goal was to render arbitrary real algebraic surfaces interactively on an iPhone and iPad using **OpenGL ES 2.0**.
An implicit real algebraic surface $\mathcal{S} \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ is the zero-level set of a trivariate polynomial $f(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{R}[x, y, z]$ of degree $d$:
$$\mathcal{S} = \left\{ (x, y, z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 \;\middle|\; f(x, y, z) = \sum_{i+j+k \le d} c_{ijk} \, x^i y^j z^k = 0 \right\}$$
Unlike standard 3D game assets (cars, characters, architecture) modeled as explicit triangle meshes in Blender or Maya, algebraic surfaces are defined purely by mathematical equations:
* **Steiner's Roman Surface** ($d = 4$): $x^2 y^2 + y^2 z^2 + z^2 x^2 - 2xyz = 0$ * **Kummer's Quartic** ($d = 4$, 16 double points): $(x^2+y^2+z^2-\mu^2)^2 - \lambda p q r s = 0$ * **Cayley's Nodal Cubic** ($d = 3$, 4 conical nodes): $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + x^2 z - y^2 z - 1 = 0$ * **The Barth Sextic** ($d = 6$, 65 ordinary double points): $4(\phi^2 x^2 - y^2)(\phi^2 y^2 - z^2)(\phi^2 z^2 - x^2) - (1 + 2\phi)(x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 1)^2 = 0$
The first architectural question every graphics programmer asks is: **"Why not just run Marching Cubes on the equation $f(x,y,z) = 0$ to generate a triangle mesh, upload a Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) to OpenGL ES, and rasterize it normally?"**
Here is why polygon meshes fail catastrophically for algebraic geometry—both mathematically and computationally—and why we built a **per-pixel GPU ray tracer / raymarcher** instead.
---
## 1. The Singularity Crisis: Why Marching Cubes Breaks Where $\nabla f = \mathbf{0}$
A point $\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{S}$ on an algebraic surface is **smooth (regular)** if the gradient vector does not vanish:
$$\nabla f(\mathbf{p}) = \left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(\mathbf{p}),\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(\mathbf{p}),\, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}(\mathbf{p}) \right) \neq (0, 0, 0)$$
By the Implicit Function Theorem, around any smooth point, the surface behaves locally like a flat plane with a well-defined unit normal $\mathbf{n} = \nabla f / \|\nabla f\|$.
However, the entire reason mathematicians study surfaces like the *Barth Sextic*, *Chmutov Octic*, or *Ding-Dong* ($x^2 + y^2 - z^3(1-z) = 0$) is their **singularities**—the points where $f(\mathbf{p}) = 0$ **and** $\nabla f(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{0}$ simultaneously: * **Ordinary Double Points ($A_1$ Conical Nodes)**: Two smooth cones touching tip-to-tip at a single infinitesimal point (65 of them on the Barth Sextic!). * **Cusps & Pinch Points (Whitney Umbrellas)**: Where a surface sheet folds into a razor-sharp crease or self-intersects along a line. * **Thin Sheets & Grazing Tangents**: Where $f(x,y,z)$ dips to zero and immediately rises back up without changing sign ($f(x,y,z) \ge 0$ everywhere), or changes sign twice inside a microscopic gap.
![The Barth Sextic rendered via per-pixel GPU raymarching — 65 razor-sharp conical double points preserved without mesh tearing](https://www.appzar.com.ar/assets/surfzar/studio_barth.webp)
### How Voxel Polygonization Fails at Singularities
Algorithms like **Marching Cubes** sample $f(x, y, z)$ on a uniform 3D lattice of cubes with edge length $\Delta h$. For each cube, it inspects the **8 corner signs** ($+$ or $-$) and looks up one of $2^8 = 256$ pre-triangulated topological cases, placing vertices along cube edges by linear interpolation:
$$\mathbf{v}_{\text{edge}} = \mathbf{p}_1 + \frac{-f(\mathbf{p}_1)}{f(\mathbf{p}_2) - f(\mathbf{p}_1)}(\mathbf{p}_2 - \mathbf{p}_1)$$
This assumption breaks down in three fundamental ways on algebraic surfaces:
```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph MC["Polygon Mesh Discretization (Marching Cubes)"] M1["Uniform Voxel Grid (Δh)"] --> M2["Samples Only 8 Cube Corners"] M2 --> M3["Conical Singularity (∇f = 0) Lies Inside Voxel"] M3 --> M4["Topology Collapse: Fuses Cones into a Thick Tube or Tears a Hole"] end subgraph RT["Per-Pixel Analytical Ray Tracing / Raymarching"] R1["Screen-Space Pixel Ray r(t) = o + t·d"] --> R2["Substitutes Directly into f(o + t·d) = 0"] R2 --> R3["Continuous 1D Root Solver on GPU"] R3 --> R4["Exact Hit t* & Analytical Normal ∇f(p) at Sub-Pixel Precision"] end ```
1. **Sub-Voxel Sign Cancellation**: Near a double point where two cone tips meet, the cross-section radius of the cone shrinks to zero. As soon as the cone radius is smaller than the voxel spacing $\Delta h$, both sides of the sheet pass between two adjacent grid vertices. Marching Cubes sees the **same sign** at both corners, concludes the surface does not exist in that cell, and **tears a jagged hole right where the cones should touch**. 2. **Manifold Assumption Violation**: Marching Cubes is designed to produce a 2-manifold triangle mesh. Algebraic surfaces with self-intersections (like *Steiner's Roman Surface*, where three planes intersect along the $x, y, z$ axes) are **non-manifold**. Marching Cubes forces non-manifold junctions to either separate artificially or fuse into blobby tubes. 3. **Zero-Gradient Normal Collapse**: Even if a vertex lands near a singularity, interpolating vertex normals across a triangle spanning $\nabla f \to \mathbf{0}$ produces wild shading seams and flickering specular highlights.
---
## 2. The $O(N^3)$ Memory & Real-Time Edit Wall on Mobile GPUs
Suppose you try to brute-force Marching Cubes by shrinking the voxel size $\Delta h$ so the singularities look sharper.
In 3D space, halving $\Delta h$ multiplies the number of grid cells to evaluate by **$2^3 = 8\times$** and the number of output triangles by **$2^2 = 4\times$**:
| Grid Resolution | Voxel Evaluations ($N^3$) | Approx. Triangles | Vertex + Normal VBO Size | Time to Re-Mesh on Mobile CPU | | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | | **$64^3$** | $262,144$ | $\sim 45\text{K}$ | $\sim 1.1\text{ MB}$ | $\sim 0.4\text{ s}$ (Jagged, missing spikes) | | **$128^3$** | $2,097,152$ | $\sim 180\text{K}$ | $\sim 4.3\text{ MB}$ | $\sim 3.1\text{ s}$ (Visible faceting) | | **$256^3$** | $16,777,216$ | $\sim 720\text{K}$ | $\sim 17.3\text{ MB}$ | $\sim 24.8\text{ s}$ (Unusable for live editing) | | **$512^3$** | $134,217,728$ | $\sim 2.9\text{M}$ | $\sim 69.1\text{ MB}$ | **Out of Memory / Freeze** |
In **iSurfer**, the core user experience is **interactive mathematical exploration**: * The user edits a formula or drags a parameter slider $a \in [-5, 5]$ to watch a surface morph through a topological transition (for example, watching a smooth cubic surface pinch into Cayley's 4 nodal singularities). * If every parameter change required re-evaluating $16\text{ million}$ grid points on the CPU, running Marching Cubes, allocating megabytes of vertex buffers, and uploading them over the bus via `glBufferData`, the frame rate would drop to **0.04 FPS**. * Worse, as soon as the user pinches to zoom closely into a singularity, a fixed-resolution mesh reveals ugly flat triangles—requiring a dynamic octree re-meshing pass that stalls the UI thread.
---
## 3. The GPU Ray-Tracing Paradigm: Resolution-Independent Implicit Precision
Instead of discretizing **3D object space** into millions of triangles on the CPU, per-pixel GPU ray tracing discretizes only **2D screen space** (the pixels currently visible on the display):
1. **Zero Geometry Buffers**: The vertex stage draws only a single bounding volume (a full-screen quad or bounding box/sphere of 2 to 12 triangles). Vertex memory footprint is under **1 KB**, regardless of whether the equation is a simple sphere ($x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 1 = 0$) or a degree-10 Chmutov surface with hundreds of singularities. 2. **Complexity Scales with Screen Pixels ($O(W \times H)$), Not Volume ($O(N^3)$)**: For each pixel $(u, v)$ covered by the bounding sphere, the fragment shader constructs a viewing ray in object space: $$\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, \quad t \in [t_{\text{enter}}, t_{\text{exit}}]$$ Substituting $\mathbf{r}(t)$ into $f(x, y, z) = 0$ turns the 3D surface intersection into a **1D univariate equation along the ray**: $$g(t) = f(o_x + t d_x,\, o_y + t d_y,\, o_z + t d_z) = 0$$ 3. **Infinite Zoom Without Re-Meshing**: When you pinch-zoom $100\times$ into a microscopic conical singularity of the Barth Sextic, the camera ray origin $\mathbf{o}$ and direction $\mathbf{d}$ simply narrow their field of view. The fragment shader still solves $g(t) = 0$ to floating-point precision for each screen pixel—meaning the singularity remains **razor-sharp at any magnification** with zero extra memory and zero CPU work! 4. **Exact Analytical Normals at Every Pixel**: Once the smallest positive root $t^* \in [t_{\text{enter}}, t_{\text{exit}}]$ is found, the exact hit point is $\mathbf{p}^* = \mathbf{o} + t^*\mathbf{d}$, and the fragment shader evaluates the exact symbolic gradient $\nabla f(\mathbf{p}^*)$ right at that pixel—eliminating Mach bands and specular wobble completely.
---
## Up Next in Part 2
Knowing *why* we must evaluate $f(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) = 0$ per pixel inside an OpenGL ES 2.0 fragment shader raises an immediate systems engineering challenge: **GLSL shaders are compiled programs on the GPU, not interpreted strings**. When a user types a brand-new algebraic equation on the iPhone keyboard, how do we parse it, expand its exponents and derivatives, translate it into optimized GLSL code, and compile it onto the mobile GPU on the fly in milliseconds?
Read [**iSurfer Part 2: From Touch Input to GPU Silicon — The Equation Parser & On-the-Fly GLSL Shader Compiler**](https://www.appzar.com.ar/posts/isurfer-part-2-equation-parser-ast-and-on-the-fly-glsl-compiler/).

item.title: Crypto Audio Steganography in C: Hiding AES & DES Ciphertext Inside WAV Files
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: Implementing a low-level cryptography and audio steganography tool in C that encrypts payloads with AES, DES, and SHA integrity digests and conceals the bits inside uncompressed PCM WAV audio samples.
item.content:encoded:
While cryptography focuses on making a message **unreadable** to an eavesdropper, **steganography** focuses on making the very **existence of the message invisible**. When you combine both—encrypting a secret payload with strong block ciphers and embedding the resulting ciphertext inside an innocent carrier medium—an attacker inspecting network traffic sees only an ordinary media file.
Back in 2011, Gustavo Maldonado and I built [**Crypto Audio Steganography (`cripto2011`)**](https://github.com/daniazar/cripto2011) in **C**: a command-line cryptography and steganography engine that encrypts arbitrary files using **AES** or **DES**, computes **SHA** integrity digests, and conceals the binary stream inside uncompressed **PCM `.wav` audio files**.
---
## Why Uncompressed WAV Audio Makes an Ideal Carrier
A standard CD-quality stereo `.wav` file sampled at $44.1\text{ kHz}$ with $16\text{-bit}$ signed PCM samples contains:
$$44{,}100 \times 2 \text{ channels} = 88{,}200 \text{ samples per second}$$
Because human hearing cannot perceive a $\pm 1$ quantization change in a $16\text{-bit}$ amplitude sample ($[-32768, 32767]$), replacing the **Least Significant Bit (LSB)** of each sample introduces an imperceptible noise floor at roughly $-96\text{ dB}$ while providing **$88.2\text{ kilobits}$ ($\approx 11\text{ KB}$) of covert storage capacity per second of audio**—over $1.9\text{ MB}$ of hidden payload inside a typical 3-minute song!
---
## Two-Stage Pipeline: Encrypt First, Embed Second
Embedding raw plaintext bits directly into LSB audio samples is dangerous: statistical steganalysis or simple bit-plane extraction would immediately reveal ASCII headers or file magic bytes. To prevent this, `cripto2011` enforces a strict **Encrypt-then-Embed** pipeline:
```mermaid flowchart LR A["Secret Payload File\n+ Filename Metadata"] --> B["SHA Integrity Digest\nTamper Detection"] B --> C["Block Cipher Encryption\nAES / DES (CBC / ECB)"] C --> D["Pseudo-Uniform Ciphertext\nBit-Stream Slicer"] D --> E["WAV RIFF Header Parser\nSkip 44-Byte PCM Header"] E --> F["LSB Sample Injector\nModify Bit 0 of 16-bit PCM Samples"] ```
1. **RIFF/WAV Header Parsing in C**: The parser reads the 44-byte RIFF/WAVE header cleanly in C structs, verifying that the carrier is uncompressed PCM (`AudioFormat == 1`) and calculating exact available bit capacity from `Subchunk2Size` before touching a single audio sample. 2. **Cryptographic Envelope (AES / DES + SHA)**: The secret file is hashed with **SHA** to guarantee integrity upon extraction and encrypted with **AES** or **DES** so the resulting bit-stream is statistically indistinguishable from uniform random noise. 3. **LSB Bit-Plane Injection & Extraction**: After the 44-byte WAV header, the encoder masks and replaces the least significant bit(s) of each 16-bit audio sample (`(sample & ~1) | payload_bit`). On the receiving end, the extractor reconstructs the ciphertext bit-by-bit, decrypts it with the symmetric key, and verifies the SHA digest to confirm zero bit-corruption.
The C source code is archived on GitHub at [**github.com/daniazar/cripto2011**](https://github.com/daniazar/cripto2011).

item.title: Procedural Track Generation & 2.5D Camera Physics in Early Unity 3D: City Racing & Asteroids Deluxe
item.dc:creator: Daniel Azar
item.description: How we built infinite procedurally generated city racing tracks with AI opponents (reaching 10,000+ plays on Kongregate) and a dual-camera 2D/2.5D Asteroids game in C# and Unity 3D.
item.content:encoded:
Back in 2010, during university game development and computer graphics courses at ITBA, I built two 3D games in **C# and Unity 3D**: [**City Racing**](https://www.kongregate.com/games/daniazar/city-racing) (which went on to accumulate over **10,000 plays on Kongregate**) and [**Asteroids Deluxe**](https://daniazar.github.io/ITBA-asteroids/).
Both projects were exercises in squeezing maximum replayability out of lightweight procedural systems and custom camera/physics controllers.
---
## 1. City Racing: Infinite Procedural Road Networks & Spline AI
In traditional arcade racing games, level designers spend weeks hand-modeling static tracks. For [**City Racing**](https://github.com/daniazar/ITBA-CityRace), we wanted every single race to take place on a newly generated urban circuit without ever hitting a dead end or self-intersecting road block.
```mermaid flowchart LR A["Procedural Grid & Spline Generator\nStraights, 90° Turns & City Blocks"] --> B["Dynamic Chunk Instantiation\nBuildings, Streetlights & Colliders"] B --> C["Waypoint Navigation Graph\nLookahead Steering & Speed Braking Zones"] C --> D["AI Opponent Controllers\nOvertaking + Rubber-Band Pacing"] ```
### Procedural Track & City Block Generation - **Tile & Spline Continuity**: As the player's car advanced, the track generator stitched modular road segments (straights, curves, intersections) and populated surrounding city blocks with randomized building prefabs and street props, recycling behind-camera chunks to keep memory flat. - **Waypoint-Driven AI Opponents**: Because the track didn't exist before runtime, AI opponents couldn't rely on pre-baked navmeshes. Each spawned road segment automatically registered entry, apex, and exit waypoints; AI cars calculated steering torque toward the next apex while modulating throttle based on upcoming turn curvature.
When we published **City Racing** to [**Kongregate**](https://www.kongregate.com/games/daniazar/city-racing), over **10,000 players** raced across its procedural city circuits.
---
## 2. Asteroids Deluxe: Dual-Perspective 2D Classic vs. 2.5D Chase Camera
For [**Asteroids Deluxe**](https://github.com/daniazar/ITBA-asteroids), the goal was to take Atari's 1979 vector classic and reimagine how perspective changes spatial awareness without altering the underlying Newtonian drift physics:
- **2D Classic Orthographic Mode**: A top-down orthographic camera replicating the classic arcade wrap-around playfield where players judge asteroid trajectories across all 360 degrees simultaneously. - **2.5D Third-Person Chase Mode**: With a single keypress, the camera smoothly interpolated behind the spacecraft into a 3D perspective chase view. Firing thrusters and weaving through rotating 3D asteroid fields suddenly felt like a cockpit dogfight, even though the rigid-body momentum and toroidal screen-wrapping rules remained identical under the hood.
In 2016, I migrated the original Unity 2.x/3.x C# codebases to Unity 5 WebGL so [**Asteroids Deluxe can be played directly in modern browsers**](https://daniazar.github.io/ITBA-asteroids/).
